opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
"Lord, I am not worthy that You should enter under my roof, but only say the word and my soul shall be healed."

Several years ago, the structure of the Mass changed, and before receiving the Eucharist, we now pray, "Lord, I am not worthy that You should enter under my roof, but only say the word and my soul shall be healed." These words are adapted from the words of the Roman centurion in the Gospel of Matthew and the Gospel of Luke. The centurion says, "my servant shall be healed." The Church places us in his position, but instead of asking for another person's healing, we ask for our own. Before receiving Christ, we acknowledge that the deepest healing we need is not of the body but of the soul.

I suppose our soul is our servant, or perhaps more accurately, the Lord's servant. Almost as if we are asking that our soul be healed so that it may truly serve God and do His will. Yet I also wonder if perhaps the soul is not the servant at all. What if we are? What if we are really saying, "Lord, heal the deepest part of me, because unless my self is healed, I cannot become Your servant?" Healing is not the end. Healing prepares us for mission. The Eucharist is never simply medicine for ourselves; it is nourishment for a life given away in love.

The centurion recognized authority. He understood that Christ's word reaches where human effort cannot. He did not ask Jesus to come into his home. He simply trusted that Christ's word alone possessed the power to heal. We often try to heal ourselves through self-improvement, analysis, discipline, or control. The centurion simply trusted: "Only say the word."

I believe our soul is light. It is beautiful. It is not created to find fault. The soul itself is not corrupted. It is wounded by sin but remains the image of God. It is our human condition that distorts the soul's purpose. Our intellect, emotions, memories, habits, fears, and even our brain influence how that soul expresses itself. Our brains see, interpret, speak, and decipher the world through already defined formulations. Everything we experience becomes filtered through memories, learned responses, preconceived ideas, and conditioned ways of thinking.

What if we did not have those imprints? What if we were simply born without them? What type of people would we be? I sometimes wonder if much of what we call "ourselves" is actually a collection of conditioned responses. We control our brains so much with predefined learned behaviors that we no longer know who we truly are. We have lessened our purpose—perhaps even God's purpose for us.

This raises a deeper question: Who am I underneath all of my conditioning?

Modern neuroscience would answer that we are the product of genetics, memory, learning, and environment. Christianity answers differently. We are first beloved children of God. Everything else comes afterward. Holiness is not the absence of experience. Holiness is complete openness to God. That openness is what Christ came to restore.

Scripture speaks about renewal rather than replacement. St. Paul writes, "Be transformed by the renewal of your mind." He does not say to discard the mind. He says it must be renewed. The brain learns habits. The soul receives grace. Over time, grace begins teaching the brain new habits until they become one movement.

Perhaps that is why so many of us feel divided. St. Paul himself speaks of this struggle: "I do not do the good I want, but the evil I do not want is what I do." He was not describing two souls. He was describing a divided person. We almost exist as two different people. There is the person formed by experience, habit, fear, expectations, pride, wounds, and ego—the false self. Then there is the true self, the person God eternally knows. Much of life is spent defending a self that does not really exist. The spiritual journey is not about inventing a better version of ourselves. It is allowing the false self to die so the true self can emerge.

How then do we free ourselves from these preexisting states, responses, and reflexes? How do we exist without having someone tell us how to preexist? Not by trying to erase the brain, but by allowing grace to reorder it. Not through greater effort alone, but through surrender.

Perhaps what can be done is simpler than we imagine. We spend time in silence before Christ, especially in Eucharistic adoration. We notice our automatic reactions without immediately identifying with them. We ask ourselves, "Is this fear speaking, or is this love?" We read the Gospels not simply for information but to watch how Jesus sees people. Instead of praying, "Lord, help me become who I want to be," perhaps we pray, "Lord, reveal who You already created me to be." That prayer assumes God is not building someone new out of us. He is uncovering someone who has been there all along.

Our Heavenly Father exists within our soul, although perhaps buried more deeply for some than for others. Over time, we accumulate so much noise, so many learned responses, so many ways of thinking, that we almost become two different people. The question is not whether God is present. The question is how we remove everything that has covered what He has already placed within us.

Perhaps that is what this prayer is asking every time we approach the Eucharist. Christ speaks the word, our soul is healed, and we are sent to live not according to our old conditioning but according to the life of God already planted within us. We come before Him not because we have perfected ourselves, but because we recognize that His word alone possesses the authority to heal the deepest part of us.

"Lord, I am not worthy that You should enter under my roof, but only say the word and my soul shall be healed."
